title: The first way (ST I.2.3)
hook: change needs a source that isn't itself changed

segments.voice: Yesterday, can we prove God? Thomas said reason can reach that God is, working back from the world, but not all that God is. Your line was reason can reach. What hard question got your five minutes? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-six.

A pot of water sits on the stove. Cold. It could be hot; it just isn't yet. Then the burner catches, and slowly the could-be becomes is. Small bubbles at the bottom, then a rolling boil. The water didn't heat itself. Something already hot had to do it. That's almost too plain to say out loud. But Thomas Aquinas builds his first argument for God on exactly that plainness. In the Summa he calls it the more obvious way, because it starts from something nobody can miss: things change. Today's word is that first way.
screen: `COLD WATER ON THE STOVE.` → `IT DIDN'T HEAT ITSELF.` → `THINGS CHANGE.`

segments.voice: First, a word Thomas uses: motion. For him it means more than traveling across a room. It means any change, a could-be becoming an is. Cold water getting hot. A seed becoming a tree. Second, the rule. Nothing gets from could-be to is on its own. It needs something that already is. Thomas's own example is fire: fire, actually hot, makes wood, which could be hot, actually hot. And the same thing can't be giving and receiving the same heat at once. So whatever is changed is changed by another. Third, the chain. Thomas pictures a hand moving a staff, and the staff moving something else. The staff moves only because the hand moves it. Now suppose every link were like the staff: only passing along motion it got from somewhere else, with no source anywhere. Then nothing would move at all. A thousand sticks, and no hand, push nothing. So, Thomas says, we have to come to a first mover, moved by no other, and this everyone understands to be God. Now a careful point. Thomas is not walking back through time to a first push at the start of the world. Later in the Summa he says that reason alone can't prove the world had a beginning; that, he says, is held by faith. His own example points to a chain right now, like hand and staff: what is moving things at this moment. And unmoved doesn't mean frozen, like a statue. It means God has no could-be left. Nothing in God is waiting to become. The letter of James says it in the Douay-Rheims: the Father of lights, "with whom there is no change, nor shadow of alteration."
screen: `MOTION MEANS ANY CHANGE.` · `NOTHING CHANGES ITSELF.` · `NO HAND, NO MOVING STAFF.` · `A CHAIN NOW, NOT A FIRST PUSH.` · then, large: `NO CHANGE, NOR SHADOW OF ALTERATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch something move. Settle, and breathe. Find one moving thing. A curtain in a draft. Steam from a cup. Leaves outside the window. Your own chest, rising and falling. Watch it without naming anything at first. Then ask what's moving it. The air. And what's moving the air? Take it back one link, and another, slowly, and notice that every link you find is leaning on something else. If you pray, you can rest at the end of the chain with the one Thomas calls the first mover. If you don't, just keep watching the thing move. The bell holds the time.
The first way. Thomas's argument from change: whatever changes is changed by another, and the chain must rest on a first mover, moved by nothing. Today's word.
Your line: the unmoved mover. Today, when you flip a switch or start the car, ask once what's moving the thing that moves it. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-six.

screen: `DAY 1156 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SECOND AND THIRD WAYS.`

howItsDone: Catholic philosophy courses often begin Thomas's five ways with the argument from motion, reading his hand-and-staff chain as what moves things now, not a first moment in time.

fork.setup: a hand moves a staff, and the staff moves a stone. the staff only moves because the hand moves it. what does Thomas say about a chain like this?
options: each link could move itself if it tried.
it can run on forever with no source at all.
it has to rest on a first mover, moved by no other.
fork.reveal: with no first mover, no link would move at all: sticks with no hand push nothing. Thomas says this first mover everyone understands to be God.

original.note: Latin: the first mover — Thomas's phrase in the first way, a first mover moved by no other.

trapdoor: what you thought: God gave the world a push once, long ago, and stepped back.
what it means: whatever changes is changed by another, and the chain needs a source, moved by nothing, holding it now.
what a scholar hears: motion as potency becoming act; an ordered chain like hand and staff, not a series in time, since Thomas says reason can't prove the world began (ST I.46.2).
recall: toward God, for his own sake

sources.ref: Summa Theologiae I, q. 2, a. 3 (the first way)

notes: ST I.2.3 first way paraphrased: 'the first and more manifest way'; motion as reduction from potentiality to actuality; fire and wood; nothing both mover and moved in the same respect; staff moved by the hand; no infinite regress; 'this everyone understands to be God'. Confirm.

ST I.46.2 paraphrased: that the world began cannot be demonstrated, and is held by faith alone. The script uses this to say the first way is not an argument back through time; some Thomists frame the per se / per accidens distinction differently. Confirm the framing.
'Unmoved doesn't mean frozen ... God has no could-be left' is an explanatory gloss (God as pure act); confirm it is fair.
Douay-Rheims James 1:17: confirm exact wording ('with whom there is no change, nor shadow of alteration').
The chain-now reading follows Thomas's own staff-and-hand example.
